text: Last spring the Harmon City public library extended its opening hours on Saturdays and Sundays. Over the following six months, the number of visits to the library rose by 20 percent compared with the same months a year earlier. The library's director concludes that the longer weekend hours were responsible for the increase, and she recommends extending weekday hours as well in order to attract still more visitors.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's conclusion?
options: Several neighboring towns have also considered extending the opening hours of their libraries.
Most of the additional visits took place on weekday afternoons, when the library's hours had not changed.
The cost of staffing the library on weekends rose after the new hours began.
Library visits in Harmon City had fallen slightly in each of the three years before the weekend hours were extended.
Some residents who visit the library on weekends also visit it during the week.
explanation: The director credits the new weekend hours with the rise in visits. If most of the extra visits happened on weekday afternoons, when nothing about the hours changed, the weekend extension cannot account for much of the increase. The earlier decline in (D) does not show that something else caused the recent rise, and the staffing cost in (C) is about money, not about why visits increased.

text: Researchers followed 2,000 office workers for one year. The workers who took a short walk after lunch on at least four days a week reported far fewer afternoon headaches than the workers who rarely walked after lunch. Both groups worked in the same buildings and held similar jobs. The researchers conclude that a short walk after lunch helps to prevent afternoon headaches.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?
options: Some of the workers who rarely walked after lunch exercised in the evening instead.
Workers who walked after lunch also tended to drink more water in the afternoon than those who did not.
When workers who had rarely walked began walking after lunch, their headaches declined.
Afternoon headaches are among the complaints most often reported by office workers.
A few of the workers left the study before the year was over.
explanation: The study shows only a link between walking and fewer headaches. Evidence that headaches dropped when the same people started walking makes it much more likely that the walking itself is the cause. (B) is the trap: it offers another possible cause, drinking more water, so it weakens the conclusion instead of strengthening it.

text: The owners of Lindqvist Bakery plan to stop printing paper receipts and to offer receipts by email instead. They argue that the change will lower the bakery's costs, because the bakery now spends a noticeable sum each month on receipt paper and printer ink, while sending an email costs almost nothing. They also expect customers to welcome the change, since it will reduce paper waste.

stem: The owners' argument that the change will lower costs depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most of the bakery's regular customers would rather receive their receipts by email than on paper.
Other bakeries in the area have already stopped printing paper receipts.
Customers will buy more bread once the bakery stops printing receipts.
Running an email receipt system will not cost the bakery more than it now spends on paper and ink.
The price of receipt paper will rise sharply over the coming year.
explanation: The owners compare the cost of paper and ink with the cost of sending an email, but an email system may have other costs, such as software fees or staff time. The argument needs those costs to stay below what the bakery now spends on paper; if they did not, the change would not save money. (A) concerns whether customers welcome the change, which is a separate claim from the cost argument.

text: After the town of Ostrava Falls installed much brighter LED streetlights on its main roads, the number of nighttime traffic accidents on those roads fell, as officials had hoped. During the same period, however, the number of nighttime accidents on the town's side streets, where the older and dimmer lights remained, rose noticeably. The amount of nighttime traffic on the side streets did not change.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Eyes adjusted to bright light see poorly for several seconds in a dimly lit street.
Main roads in Ostrava Falls carry considerably more traffic at night than the town's side streets do.
The LED streetlights use less electricity than the lights they replaced.
Accidents on side streets are usually less serious than accidents on main roads.
The town plans to install LED lights on its side streets within five years.
explanation: The puzzle is why accidents rose on side streets whose lights did not change. If drivers coming off the brightly lit main roads cannot see well for a few seconds in the dimmer side streets, the new lights could indirectly make side streets more dangerous. (B) is true but explains nothing about a change, and the passage already rules out more side-street traffic as the cause.

text: For many years, historians held that the coastal town of Merovar was abandoned because violent storms in the 1290s filled its harbor with silt. Dr. Amara Okafor rejects this view. She points out that tax records show the town's population falling sharply in the 1250s, decades before the storms, and she concludes that the condition of the harbor played no part in the town's abandonment.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens Dr. Okafor's conclusion?
options: Merovar's tax records for the 1250s are more complete than the town's records for any other decade.
Several other coastal towns in the region were also abandoned during the 1300s.
The storms of the 1290s were the most violent recorded in the region during that century.
Some families who left Merovar in the 1250s settled in farming villages farther inland.
Records from nearby ports show that Merovar's harbor had begun filling with silt in the 1240s.
explanation: Dr. Okafor reasons that because the decline began before the storms, the harbor did not matter. But if the harbor was already silting up in the 1240s, its condition could explain the early fall in population, so her conclusion that the harbor played no part is undermined. (C) only stresses how strong the storms were, which does not touch the problem that the decline began earlier.

text: Many analysts predicted that Fernhill Motors' new electric scooter would sell poorly, because its price is higher than the prices of rival models. ⟦In its first year on the market, however, the scooter outsold every rival in its class.⟧ The main reason is probably its battery, which lasts nearly twice as long as the batteries of competing scooters: ⟦buyers who ride long distances every day have been willing to pay more to avoid recharging during the day.⟧

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is a prediction that the argument accepts as accurate; the second is evidence that is offered in support of that prediction.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is a consideration that weighs against that conclusion.
The first is a fact that runs contrary to a prediction; the second is part of an explanation the argument offers for that fact.
The first is evidence offered in support of the analysts' view; the second is a restatement of that view.
The first is a fact that the argument seeks to explain; the second is an objection to the explanation the argument gives.
explanation: The first portion reports what actually happened, and it contradicts the analysts' prediction of poor sales. The second portion explains why buyers paid the higher price, so it is part of the argument's explanation of the strong sales. (E) gets the first portion right but wrongly calls the second an objection; it supports the explanation instead of challenging it.

text: A survey covered 400 laboratories in universities, hospitals, and private companies. Every laboratory that had adopted a shared electronic notebook system reported losing fewer data files than in the previous year. None of the laboratories that reported losing fewer data files had reduced its staff during the year. Some of the laboratories that reduced staff, however, reported spending more time on record keeping.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: None of the surveyed laboratories that adopted the shared notebook system reduced its staff.
Every laboratory that reported losing fewer data files had adopted the shared notebook system.
The laboratories that reduced staff lost more data files than they had the year before.
The shared notebook system reduces the time that laboratories spend on record keeping.
Most of the surveyed laboratories adopted the shared notebook system during the year.
explanation: Chain the statements: adopting the system means losing fewer files, and losing fewer files means not reducing staff, so no laboratory that adopted the system reduced its staff. (B) reverses the first statement; other laboratories could also have lost fewer files. (C) goes too far: laboratories that cut staff did not lose fewer files, but they might have lost the same number as before.

text: The city of Vale Rosa plans to charge drivers a fee for entering the old city center during weekday business hours. Officials argue that the fee will reduce traffic congestion in the center, because many drivers will choose to take the bus or the tram rather than pay. Money raised by the fee would be spent on repairing the center's narrow streets.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the officials' argument?
options: Whether the old city center has more shops than other parts of Vale Rosa
How many tourists visit the old city center on weekends, when the fee will not be charged
Whether the fee will be collected by cameras or by toll booths
Whether the fee will be high enough to persuade many drivers to change how they travel
How long ago the tram line to the old city center was built
explanation: The argument rests on the claim that many drivers will switch to the bus or tram instead of paying. Whether the fee is large enough to change drivers' behavior decides whether that claim holds: a small fee might simply be paid. (B) is tempting because it mentions visitor numbers, but the fee applies only on weekdays, so weekend tourists are irrelevant.

text: A software company found that its programmers who used a new code-checking tool made 40 percent fewer errors per month than the programmers who did not use it. Use of the tool had been voluntary, and each programmer decided whether to try it. The company's managers concluded that the tool reduces programming errors, and they decided to require every programmer to use it.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' conclusion?
options: The tool costs the company a small fee for each programmer every month.
The programmers who chose the tool were mostly experienced ones, who already made few errors.
Some programmers who used the tool said that it slowed down their work.
Errors found after software is released are much more costly to fix than errors found earlier.
The company plans to hire more programmers next year.
explanation: Because programmers chose for themselves, the two groups may have differed from the start. If the tool users were mainly experienced programmers who already made few errors, their lower error rate could reflect experience rather than the tool. (C) is a complaint about speed and says nothing about whether the tool reduces errors.

text: Pottery fragments found at a site in the Ardena Valley are decorated with a spiral pattern otherwise known only from the coastal settlement of Thalos, more than 200 kilometers away. The fragments date from the same century as the earliest decorated pottery at Thalos. The archaeologist Chen Wei argues that the people of the valley traded with Thalos rather than developing the pattern on their own.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens Chen Wei's argument?
options: The spiral pattern is simple enough that many ancient peoples could have invented it.
Pottery made at Thalos has also been found at several sites along the coast.
The Ardena Valley site contains more pottery fragments than any other excavated site in the region.
Spiral patterns appear on some of the earliest pottery made anywhere in the world.
Chemical analysis shows that the clay of the decorated fragments came from deposits near Thalos.
explanation: If the clay itself came from near Thalos, the pots were most likely made there and carried to the valley, which is strong evidence of contact through trade. (A) and (D) point the other way, since they make independent invention more plausible. (B) shows that Thalos traded along the coast but says nothing about the Ardena Valley.

text: A hospital in Porto Verde began sending text-message reminders to patients on the day before their appointments. In the following year, the share of patients who missed their appointments fell from 18 percent to 11 percent. The hospital's administrator credits the reminders with the improvement and plans to begin sending the same reminders to patients of the hospital's dental clinic, expecting a similar drop in missed appointments there.

stem: The administrator's plan for the dental clinic depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The dental clinic's rate of missed appointments is higher than that of any other part of the hospital.
Text-message reminders cost the hospital less to send than reminder letters would.
The hospital will eventually stop sending reminders to patients of its other departments.
A substantial share of the dental clinic's patients have phones that can receive text messages.
Missed appointments cost the hospital more than any other kind of scheduling problem.
explanation: Reminders can only work for patients who receive them. If few dental patients could get text messages, the plan could not produce a similar drop, so the administrator must assume that many of them can. (A) is not needed: the plan could work even if the dental clinic's rate were average. (B) concerns cost, which the plan's expected result does not depend on.

text: Last year, the bookstore chain Sundara Books cut the price of every paperback it sells by 15 percent. Over the following year, the number of paperbacks the chain sold rose by 30 percent, more than enough to make up for the lower price. Nevertheless, the chain's total profit from book sales fell during the year, even though its costs for rent and staff did not change.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain how the chain's profit from book sales could have fallen?
options: Other bookstore chains did not reduce the prices of their paperbacks last year.
Many customers switched from the chain's high-profit hardcover editions to its paperbacks.
The chain sold more paperbacks during the holiday season than at any other time of the year.
Some customers bought more paperbacks than they had planned to because of the lower prices.
The chain's costs for rent and staff are higher than those of most independent bookstores.
explanation: Paperback revenue rose, so the fall in profit must come from somewhere else in book sales. If customers switched from high-profit hardcovers to cheaper paperbacks, the chain lost more on hardcovers than it gained on paperbacks. (D) explains why paperback sales rose, which is not the puzzle, and (E) describes costs the passage says did not change.

text: In a recent study, older mice that were fed a diet containing a blueberry extract found their way through a maze faster than older mice that were fed an ordinary diet. The two groups were otherwise treated identically. On the basis of this study, a health magazine advises older adults to eat a cup of fresh blueberries every day in order to improve their memory.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the magazine's advice?
options: Matching the mice's dose would require a person to eat several kilograms of blueberries a day.
Mice are often used in studies of memory because their brains age relatively quickly.
Blueberries are more expensive than many other fruits sold in supermarkets.
Some of the mice fed the extract did no better in the maze than the average mouse that was fed an ordinary diet.
The magazine has published advice about diet and memory several times before.
explanation: The magazine assumes that a cup of blueberries gives people the benefit the extract gave the mice. If the mice received a dose equal to several kilograms of berries a day, a single cup is unlikely to have any comparable effect. (D) is weaker: a group average can improve even when some individuals do not.

text: Some city council members argue that the city should stop paying for its free summer concerts, since the money could be spent on road repairs instead. ⟦This proposal is shortsighted.⟧ A survey of local businesses found that restaurants and shops near the concert park take in nearly a third more money on concert evenings than on other summer evenings, and ⟦the extra sales tax they collect brings the city more money than the concerts cost.⟧

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is a proposal that the argument defends; the second is a consequence of adopting that proposal.
The first is evidence offered in support of a conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
The first is a consideration raised against the argument's position; the second is the argument's reply to that consideration.
The first states a view that the argument goes on to reject; the second is an objection to that view.
The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered in support of that conclusion.
explanation: The first portion is the author's own judgment of the council members' proposal, and everything after it is given as a reason for that judgment, so it is the main conclusion. The second portion, that the concerts bring in more tax than they cost, supports it. (A) is the trap: the argument rejects the proposal to stop funding the concerts rather than defending it.

text: Over the past five years, the share of households in Kestrel County with high-speed internet access rose from 40 percent to 75 percent. Over the same period, the county's unemployment rate fell by half. A county official concludes that the spread of high-speed internet access was the main reason for the fall in unemployment and urges neighboring counties to expand access as well.

stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
options: draws a conclusion about every county in the region from figures that describe only Kestrel County
assumes that high-speed internet access will continue to spread at the same rate
takes for granted that because two changes happened together, one of them caused the other
fails to say how many households in the county still lack high-speed internet access
treats a decrease in unemployment as though it were an increase in wages
explanation: The official observes that internet access rose while unemployment fell and simply concludes that the first caused the second, ignoring other possible causes such as a general economic recovery. (A) is tempting because of the advice to other counties, but the conclusion itself is about Kestrel County, and the passage does give the share of households without access (25 percent), so (D) is wrong too.

text: The hotel chain Grünwald Hotels found that guests who booked their rooms through the chain's own website rated their stays more highly than guests who booked through travel agencies. The chain's marketing director concludes that the pleasant booking experience on the website puts guests in a better frame of mind, and she proposes spending heavily to improve the website further.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director's conclusion?
options: Booking through travel agencies costs the chain a fee for each reservation that is made.
The chain's website was last redesigned two years ago.
Some guests who book through travel agencies visit the chain's website first in order to compare prices.
Ratings of hotel stays tend to be higher in summer than in winter.
Most guests who book on the chain's website are returning guests who already liked its hotels.
explanation: The director assumes the website causes the higher ratings. If website bookers are mostly returning guests who already liked the hotels, the higher ratings reflect who books online, not the booking experience. (D) would matter only if website bookings were concentrated in summer, and the passage gives no reason to think so.

text: Records from the port of Saldanha show that in 1820 every ship that arrived from the north carried timber, salt, or both. Every ship that carried salt that year paid a harbor tax, while ships that carried only timber paid none. Ships from other directions carried a wide variety of goods. The port's accounts show that the Albatros, which arrived from the north in 1820, paid no harbor tax.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Every ship that paid no harbor tax in 1820 had arrived from the north.
The Albatros carried timber but no salt.
No ship that carried timber paid a harbor tax in 1820.
The Albatros made more than one voyage to Saldanha in 1820.
Most of the ships that arrived at Saldanha in 1820 carried salt.
explanation: Any ship carrying salt paid the tax, so the Albatros, which paid none, carried no salt. Since every northern ship carried timber, salt, or both, the Albatros must have carried timber. (C) is the trap: a ship carrying both timber and salt would have paid the tax, so timber ships did not all go untaxed.

text: Engineers at a power company propose covering parts of the company's reservoirs with floating solar panels. Water from the reservoirs is used both for drinking and for cooling the company's power plants. The engineers argue that, in addition to producing electricity, the panels would reduce the amount of water the reservoirs lose to evaporation, because the panels would shade the water from direct sunlight.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the engineers' argument?
options: Floating solar panels cost more to install than panels of the same size mounted on land.
Some of the reservoirs already have small areas covered by floating water plants.
Wind blowing across a reservoir's surface also adds considerably to the amount of water that evaporates from it.
In tests, shaded tanks of water lost far less to evaporation than unshaded tanks in the same weather.
The company's reservoirs supply drinking water to several large towns.
explanation: The argument's key claim is that shade cuts evaporation. A direct test showing that shaded water evaporates much less than unshaded water in the same conditions supports that claim. (C) mentions evaporation but names a second cause the panels are not said to affect, so it does nothing to support the engineers.

text: A team of ecologists counted songbirds in a forest before and after a highway was built along one edge of it. After the highway opened, the number of songbirds nesting within 300 meters of the road fell by half, while the number nesting deeper in the forest did not change. The team concludes that traffic noise drives songbirds away from nesting sites near busy roads.

stem: The team's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Building the highway did not destroy much of the nesting habitat within 300 meters of the road.
Songbirds are more common in the forest than any other kind of bird.
Traffic on the highway is heavier during the day than it is at night.
The songbirds that left the area near the road moved to nesting sites deeper in the forest.
Traffic noise affects all kinds of forest birds in the same way.
explanation: If construction had cleared much of the habitat near the road, the birds may have left because their nesting sites were gone, not because of noise. The conclusion therefore requires that the habitat largely survived. (D) is not required, and in fact the unchanged numbers deeper in the forest suggest the birds did not simply move there.

text: When the city of Brennick raised the fine for parking illegally downtown from $30 to $80, officials expected the number of parking tickets issued downtown to fall, since fewer drivers would risk the higher fine. Instead, over the following year the number of tickets issued downtown rose by 25 percent. The number of parking spaces downtown and the amount of traffic there stayed about the same.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the number of tickets rose?
options: Most drivers who receive parking tickets in Brennick pay them on time.
The fine for parking illegally in other parts of the city did not change.
When the fine was raised, the city also hired more officers to patrol downtown for illegal parking.
Illegally parked cars in the downtown area make it harder for delivery trucks to stop and unload their goods.
Some drivers who used to park downtown now take the bus instead.
explanation: The number of tickets depends not only on how many drivers park illegally but also on how many are caught. More patrol officers could catch a larger share of a smaller number of offenders, so tickets could rise even if illegal parking fell. (E) points the wrong way: fewer drivers downtown should mean fewer tickets.

text: Two years ago, the grocery chain Okonkwo Markets began offering free delivery on all online orders over $50. Since then, the chain's online sales have tripled, while sales in its stores have fallen only slightly. The chain's finance director argues that offering free delivery has been profitable for the company, because the increase in online sales is far larger than the decline in store sales.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the finance director's argument?
options: Online orders at the chain are, on average, somewhat larger than purchases made in its stores.
Some of the customers who now order online also continue to shop in the chain's stores every week or so.
The chain's store sales had been falling slightly for several years before free delivery was offered.
Delivering a typical online order costs the chain more than the profit it makes on the goods in that order.
Online grocery sales across the country rose by about 10 percent over the same two years.
explanation: The director treats a rise in sales as proof of profit, but sales are not profit. If each delivery costs more than the chain earns on the order, every extra online sale loses money, so free delivery could be unprofitable however much sales grow. (E) is the trap: a modest national rise does not explain a tripling, and in any case it concerns the cause of the growth, not whether the growth made money.

text: In Lunari Province, the rate of hip fractures among people over 70 fell by 20 percent in the decade after doctors began routinely prescribing vitamin D supplements to older patients. Health officials conclude that the supplements caused the decline. Critics point out that the number of people over 70 in the province grew during the decade, but because the figure the officials cite is a rate rather than a total, that growth does not affect their comparison.

stem: The health officials' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A substantial share of the older patients who were prescribed the supplements actually took them.
Hip fractures among people over 70 were already more common in Lunari than in any neighboring province.
Vitamin D supplements cause no harmful side effects in people over the age of 70.
The number of people over 70 living in Lunari did not grow during the decade.
Most hip fractures among older people are the result of falls that happen at home.
explanation: A prescription can lower fractures only if patients take the pills. If almost none of them did, the supplements could not have caused the decline, so the officials must assume many patients took them. (D) is the trap: the passage itself explains that population growth does not matter for a rate, so the argument does not need it. (C) concerns safety, which is irrelevant to whether the supplements worked.

text: Astronomers at a mountain observatory report that the sharpness of their images has improved steadily over the past decade. During the same decade, light from the growing town in the valley below has made the night sky above the observatory noticeably brighter, and a brighter sky normally makes astronomical images worse. The observatory has used the same telescope throughout the decade.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox described above?
options: Most of the town's newer street lighting points downward and is switched off after midnight.
Observatories at several other sites have also reported brighter night skies over the past decade.
The observatory now shares its images with universities in several other countries.
The population of the town in the valley has grown by about a third during the decade.
The observatory added a system that corrects blurring by the atmosphere, formerly the main limit on its images.
explanation: The images became sharper even though one factor, sky brightness, got worse. If the observatory removed a larger source of blur, atmospheric distortion, the gain could outweigh the loss from the brighter sky. (A) is tempting, but the passage states that the sky did become brighter, so less polluting lights cannot explain why the images still improved.

text: The city of Marisol plans to plant 10,000 street trees in its poorer neighborhoods, which have few trees. City officials argue that the trees will lower summer temperatures in those neighborhoods and so reduce the number of residents who need hospital treatment for heat illness. Critics object that a newly planted tree provides little shade for at least a decade, so the plan will do nothing for residents in the near future.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' argument against the critics' objection?
options: Heat illness is more common among older residents of Marisol than among younger residents.
Many residents of the poorer neighborhoods have said that they would prefer new parks to street trees.
Young trees cool the air around them by releasing water from their leaves, within two or three years of planting.
Trees planted along streets sometimes damage the pavement with their roots as they grow larger.
Most hospital visits for heat illness in Marisol take place during a few very hot weeks in the middle of each summer.
explanation: The critics assume that trees cool a street only through shade. If young trees cool the air by releasing water within a few years, the plan can help long before the trees are large, which answers the objection directly. (E) describes when heat illness occurs but says nothing about how soon the trees could make a difference.

text: ⟦Sales of printed maps have fallen by more than half over the past decade⟧, and some publishers have concluded that the printed map has no future. This conclusion is premature. ⟦Sales of printed maps for hiking and cycling have risen during the same period⟧, and because such maps are used in places where phone batteries run down and signals fail, they meet a need that digital maps cannot easily fill. Publishers who specialize in these maps are therefore likely to prosper.

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered against that conclusion.
The first is evidence offered for a conclusion the argument rejects; the second is evidence the argument uses to support its own conclusion.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its own conclusion; the second is a consideration that the argument concedes weighs against that conclusion.
The first is a judgment that the argument accepts; the second is a prediction that the argument goes on to reject.
The first and the second are both evidence offered in support of the view that the printed map has no future.
explanation: The overall fall in sales is the basis for some publishers' view that printed maps have no future, a view the argument calls premature. The rise in hiking and cycling maps is the argument's own evidence for its conclusion that specialist publishers will prosper. (C) reverses the roles: the argument does not use the overall decline to support its own position.

text: Last year the city of Ardmore replaced the paper timetables at its bus stops with a smartphone app that shows the location of every bus in real time. Records show that the buses ran no more punctually in the year after the change than in the year before. Yet complaints about late buses fell by 60 percent. The transit authority concludes that riders who can see when their bus will arrive are much less bothered by delays.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit authority's conclusion?
options: Some riders do not own smartphones and still rely on printed notices posted at the bus stops.
Riders who use the app check it an average of three times during each journey.
Since the change, complaints can be made only through a feedback page in the app that many riders cannot find.
Bus delays in Ardmore are caused mainly by heavy traffic in the city center during the morning and evening rush hours.
Complaints from riders about crowded buses rose slightly over the same year.
explanation: The authority reads fewer complaints as a sign that riders mind delays less. If complaining became much harder at the same time, the drop could reflect the new process rather than any change in riders' feelings. (E) does not help the critic: if anything, a rise in other complaints suggests riders were still able to complain.

text: A transport survey of 600 households in the town of Kerava found that 450 of the households own at least one car and 300 own at least one bicycle. Every household that owns a bicycle but no car lives within two kilometers of the town center. Households that own neither a car nor a bicycle were asked how their members travel to work. The town council will use the survey to plan new bicycle lanes.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Most of the households in the survey that own a bicycle live within two kilometers of the town center.
No surveyed household that lives more than two kilometers from the town center owns a bicycle.
Some of the households in the survey own neither a car nor a bicycle.
Households that own a car are less likely to own a bicycle than other households are.
At least 150 of the surveyed households own both a car and a bicycle.
explanation: There are only 600 households, so 450 car owners and 300 bicycle owners must overlap by at least 450 + 300 − 600 = 150. (C) is the trap: the question to households owning neither does not show that any exist, since 300 car-only, 150 both and 150 bicycle-only households would fill all 600. (B) fails because households owning both a car and a bicycle may live anywhere.

text: A museum has displayed a portrait as the work of the eighteenth-century painter Ilse Brandt for more than a century. A curator now argues that it is a later copy. Her evidence is that the canvas was woven on a type of mechanical loom that, according to the manufacturer's records, did not come into use until 1810, twelve years after Brandt's death.

stem: Which of the following would it be most useful to establish in order to evaluate the curator's argument?
options: Whether the paint could have been moved from an older canvas onto a newer one during a restoration
Whether Brandt's other paintings sold for high prices during her lifetime
How many visitors have viewed the portrait since the museum acquired it
Whether the company that made the loom also produced looms of several other types
Whether Brandt had students who painted portraits in a style very close to her own during her lifetime
explanation: The curator dates the painting by its canvas. Restorers sometimes transfer an old paint layer to a new canvas; if that happened here, the canvas could date from after 1810 while the paint is Brandt's, and the argument would collapse. (E) is the trap: students working in Brandt's lifetime would have used canvas made before 1810, so their existence does not bear on the canvas evidence.

text: Arcelia Airlines plans to remove two rows of seats from each of its planes in order to give passengers more legroom. Although each flight will then carry fewer passengers, the airline's managers argue that the change will increase its revenue, because a survey of 2,000 recent passengers found that most of them would be willing to pay a higher fare for the extra space.

stem: The managers' argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most of Arcelia's passengers travel for business purposes rather than for pleasure.
Rival airlines will not also remove seats from their planes in order to offer more legroom.
Arcelia's planes are full, or nearly full, on most of the routes that the airline flies.
The higher fares on the remaining seats will bring in more than the removed seats would have.
Passengers have complained more about Arcelia's legroom than about any other feature of its service.
explanation: Revenue rises only if what the airline gains from higher fares outweighs what it loses by having fewer seats to sell, so the managers must assume that the gain is larger. (C) is a trap: if planes often fly with empty seats, removing seats loses even less revenue, so the argument does not need full planes. (B) is not required either, since revenue could rise even if rivals copied the change.

text: Over the past twenty years, the number of frogs living in and around Lake Varna has fallen sharply. During the same period, a pesticide used on nearby farms has been detected in the lake's water at steadily rising levels. A biologist concludes that the pesticide is the main cause of the frogs' decline and urges the regional government to ban its use near the lake.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the biologist's conclusion?
options: A fungal disease that kills frogs has been reported in several regions of the world.
Frog numbers have fallen just as sharply in mountain lakes far from farms, where the pesticide has never been found.
In one year when farmers near the lake used less of the pesticide than usual, the number of frogs in the lake rose slightly.
The pesticide breaks down more slowly in cold water than it does in warm water.
Several farms near the lake have switched to growing crops that need less water.
explanation: If frogs declined equally where the pesticide is absent, some other cause is at work, and that cause may explain the decline at Lake Varna too. (A) is weaker: it names a possible cause but gives no evidence that the disease is present near the lake. (C) actually supports the biologist.

text: Last autumn the town of Belmira opened a walk-in clinic that offers free flu vaccinations, and the number of residents vaccinated against flu rose by a third compared with the year before. The vaccine was well matched to the strains that circulated that winter. Yet the number of flu cases recorded by health workers in Belmira that winter was the highest in a decade.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
options: The clinic also tests people with flu-like symptoms, so many mild cases that once went unrecorded are now counted.
Most of the residents who were vaccinated at the new clinic were more than 65 years old.
Neighboring towns without such a clinic recorded fewer flu cases per resident that winter than Belmira did.
Some residents vaccinated at the clinic had been vaccinated by their own doctors in previous years.
Flu vaccinations are recommended every year because the strains that circulate change from one season to the next.
explanation: More vaccinations should mean fewer cases, so the record count is puzzling. If the clinic also tests people and records mild cases that used to go uncounted, the number of recorded cases can rise even if actual infections fell. (C) only deepens the puzzle, and the passage rules out a mismatched vaccine, so (E) explains nothing about this winter.

text: The historian Kofi Mensah argues that cheap printed almanacs increased literacy among farmers in the province of Ostland during the eighteenth century. His evidence is that the share of farmers who signed marriage registers with their names, rather than with a mark, rose from 20 percent to 45 percent between 1720 and 1780, the period in which almanac sellers began traveling regularly through the province.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens Mensah's argument?
options: Almanacs of the period contained weather forecasts, planting advice, and short stories.
Signing one's name requires much less skill than reading a whole page of printed text.
The number of village schools in Ostland doubled between 1720 and 1780, mostly in the farming districts.
In Ostland districts that almanac sellers rarely visited, the share of farmers signing their names barely changed.
Almanacs were also popular among merchants and craftsmen in Ostland's towns.
explanation: Mensah's evidence is only that literacy rose while almanacs spread. If literacy stayed flat where almanacs rarely reached, the rise is tied to the almanacs rather than to some province-wide change. (C) is the trap: more schools offer a rival explanation and so weaken the argument, and (B) questions whether signatures measure reading ability at all.

text: Two years ago, the province of Talvora began requiring restaurants to display their official hygiene ratings on their front doors. Since then, the number of food poisoning cases traced to restaurants in the province has fallen by 30 percent. Officials conclude that public ratings have pushed restaurants to improve their hygiene, and they propose requiring food trucks to display ratings as well.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' conclusion?
options: Some restaurants that received low ratings have closed since the rule took effect.
Food trucks in Talvora serve fewer meals each day than most of its restaurants do.
Many diners say that they check a restaurant's rating before deciding whether to eat there.
Food poisoning cases traced to meals cooked at home in Talvora also fell slightly over the same two years.
Since the rule began, the province has cut the staff who trace food poisoning cases to their source.
explanation: The officials count cases traced to restaurants. If fewer staff now trace cases, fewer cases will be linked to restaurants even if restaurant hygiene has not changed, so the drop may be a product of weaker investigation. (D) is a weaker challenge: a slight fall in home cases does not account for a 30 percent drop. (A) and (C) tend to support the officials.

text: ⟦Many engineers have assumed that self-driving delivery robots will first succeed in dense city centers, where customers live closest together.⟧ But city centers are also where sidewalks are most crowded and where theft and vandalism are most common, and both problems slow the robots down and raise their operating costs. Quiet suburbs, by contrast, have wide sidewalks and few pedestrians. ⟦It is therefore in the suburbs, not the city centers, that delivery robots are likely to prove profitable first.⟧

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
The first is a view that the argument opposes; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is a consequence said to follow from that conclusion.
The first is a view that the argument opposes; the second is evidence offered against that view.
The first is an assumption on which the argument relies; the second is a prediction that the argument rejects.
explanation: The argument introduces the engineers' assumption only to challenge it with the problems of crowded city sidewalks. The second portion, introduced by "therefore," is what all the evidence supports, so it is the main conclusion. (D) is the trap: the first role is right, but the second portion is the conclusion drawn from the evidence, not a piece of the evidence itself.

text: A business magazine surveyed the 50 most profitable companies in the country and found that 46 of them allow employees to work from home at least two days a week. A management consultant quoted in the magazine concludes that allowing employees to work from home makes companies more profitable, and she advises every company to adopt such a policy. The magazine did not survey any other companies.

stem: The consultant's reasoning is flawed because it
options: relies on a survey of too few companies to support any conclusion about them
assumes without evidence that most employees prefer to work from home
ignores whether less profitable companies are just as likely to allow work from home
confuses the profitability of a company with the number of people it employs
treats a policy that applies two days a week as though it applied every working day
explanation: The survey looks only at highly profitable companies. If most less profitable companies also let employees work from home, the policy is simply common and says nothing about profit; without that comparison the conclusion is unsupported. (A) is the trap: the survey covers all 50 companies it describes, so its size is not the problem.

text: A video-streaming company plans to lower its costs by reducing the picture quality of videos sent to subscribers' phones, which would cut the amount of data it must transmit. The company's engineers argue that the change will not cost the company any subscribers, because on a phone's small screen most viewers cannot tell the difference between the current picture quality and the lower one.

stem: The engineers' argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most of the company's subscribers watch its videos on phones rather than on televisions.
The company's main rivals will not also lower the picture quality of the videos that they send to their subscribers' phones.
Sending less data will reduce the company's costs more than any other measure it could take.
Viewers who watch on phones care more about the subscription price than about picture quality.
Few subscribers send video from their phones to television screens, where the lower quality would show.
explanation: The argument relies on the small screen hiding the change. If many subscribers sent phone video to large television screens, they would see the poorer picture, and the claim that no subscribers will be lost would fail; so the engineers must assume few do this. (A) is not required: the argument is only about phone viewers, however many or few there are.

text: The guild records of the medieval city of Corvenna list nearly three times as many weavers in 1400 as in 1350. The historian Sofia Marchetti concludes that the amount of cloth produced in and around Corvenna rose greatly during that half century, and she argues that this growth explains why the city built a large new cloth hall in 1405.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens Marchetti's conclusion?
options: Cloth made in Corvenna was sold in markets throughout the region by 1400.
The population of Corvenna fell sharply in the late 1340s and had largely recovered by the year 1400.
In 1360 the guild began requiring weavers in nearby villages, who had never registered, to join.
Guild records from 1350 are kept in the same city archive as those from 1400.
The price of raw wool in Corvenna rose steadily between 1350 and 1400.
explanation: Marchetti treats a rise in registered weavers as a rise in production. If village weavers who were already working simply began to be counted after 1360, the records could triple with little change in the cloth actually made in and around the city. (B) is the trap: a population recovery is consistent with real growth in weaving, so it does not undermine the conclusion.

text: At Halvorsen Electronics, every product launched in the past five years was tested by a panel of customers before its launch. Every product that the panel rated favorably sold more than 100,000 units in its first year, although some products that the panel rated unfavorably also sold more than 100,000 units. None of the products that sold fewer than 50,000 units in their first year is still being made.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true of the products launched in the past five years?
options: Any of them that sold fewer than 50,000 units in its first year was rated unfavorably by the panel.
Every one that the panel rated unfavorably sold fewer than 100,000 units in its first year on the market.
Every one that is still being made was rated favorably by the panel.
Some that the panel rated favorably are no longer being made.
Those rated unfavorably are less likely than the others to be made today.
explanation: A favorable rating guarantees more than 100,000 first-year sales, so a product that sold fewer than 50,000 cannot have been rated favorably; it was rated unfavorably. (B) contradicts the passage, which says some unfavorably rated products sold more than 100,000. (C) and (D) may or may not be true, since the passage does not say which products are still made apart from the low sellers.

text: In the Sarnia River delta, a species of wading bird that feeds only on mudflats has become steadily more numerous over the past fifteen years. During the same period, rising sea levels have permanently flooded about a quarter of the delta's mudflats. The birds have not begun feeding anywhere else, and the number of birds that arrive from other regions has not changed.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the increase in the number of wading birds?
options: The wading birds have been protected by law from hunting throughout the region for more than fifty years.
On the remaining mudflats, the worms the birds eat have become several times more plentiful per square meter.
The mudflats that remain in the delta are covered by the tide twice each day.
Several other species of wading bird in the delta have declined over the same fifteen years.
Scientists expect the sea level in the delta to keep rising for several more decades.
explanation: The birds have less feeding ground, so they should be fewer, unless the food available to them has grown. If each square meter of the remaining mudflat now holds several times as many worms, the total food supply can rise even as the area shrinks. (A) describes protection that has been in place for fifty years, so it cannot explain a change over the last fifteen.

text: To reduce costs, the school board of Nordhaven is considering a four-day school week. Opponents argue that a shorter week will harm students' learning. Supporters reply that each of the four school days would be made longer, so that students would spend the same total number of hours in class each week as they do now, and they conclude that learning will not suffer.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the supporters' conclusion?
options: A four-day week would save the school board a large sum each year on heating and on school buses.
Most teachers in Nordhaven have said that they would prefer to work four longer days.
Students tend to be more tired near the end of a long school day than near its beginning.
Districts that moved to four longer days saw no change in test scores relative to similar districts.
Some parents would need to find child care for their children on the fifth weekday.
explanation: The supporters claim that the same hours spread over fewer days will not harm learning. Evidence that comparable districts saw no change in test scores after making the switch supports exactly that claim. (A) is the trap: it supports the case for saving money, but the conclusion at issue is about learning. (C) suggests longer days could hurt learning, so it weakens.

text: A ten-year study of 5,000 adults found that those who reported drinking at least three cups of green tea a day were 30 percent less likely to develop high blood pressure during the study than those who drank no green tea. A tea company now cites the study in advertisements that claim green tea protects drinkers against high blood pressure.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the claim made in the advertisements?
options: The tea company also sells black tea, a drink that the study did not examine.
Some of the people in the study who drank no green tea drank black tea instead.
High blood pressure becomes more common as people grow older.
The daily green tea drinkers in the study also exercised more and ate less salt than the others.
The study asked participants about their tea drinking only once, at the very start of the ten-year period.
explanation: The study shows only that tea drinkers had less high blood pressure. If the same people also exercised more and ate less salt, those habits could explain the difference, so the claim that the tea itself protects them is undermined. (E) points to imprecise measurement, but loose measurement makes a real link harder to detect rather than creating a false one.

text: Battery makers are racing to build cells that store more energy per kilogram, and ⟦the lightest batteries will probably win the market for electric aircraft.⟧ For electric delivery vans, however, weight matters far less than price and lifespan. ⟦A heavier battery that lasts through twice as many charging cycles would cost a van operator less over the life of the van⟧, so makers who focus only on lighter batteries may lose the much larger van market to their rivals.

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is a claim the argument accepts about one market; the second supports the argument's conclusion about another market.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is evidence that the argument offers in support of that conclusion.
The first is a prediction that the argument goes on to reject; the second is evidence that the argument offers against that prediction.
The first is evidence that supports the second; the second is the main conclusion that the argument draws.
The first is a consideration the argument raises against its own conclusion; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
explanation: The argument grants that light batteries will probably win in aircraft, then turns to vans, where it says other factors matter more. The second portion gives the reason makers focused only on weight may lose the van market, which is the main conclusion. (C) is the trap: the argument never rejects the aircraft prediction; it simply limits its scope, and the second portion is not the conclusion, which rules out (D) and (E).

text: The council of the seaside town of Esk Harbor plans to build a large new car park near its beach. Council members argue that a shortage of parking keeps visitors away from the town in summer, and that the extra visitors drawn by the new car park would bring more business to the town's shops and cafés. They point out that the beach's existing car parks hold only 200 cars.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the council's argument?
options: Whether the town's cafés serve fish caught by local boats
How many residents of Esk Harbor walk to the beach from their homes
Whether nearby towns have more beaches than Esk Harbor has
How much the new car park would cost compared with the town's yearly budget
Whether the beach's existing car parks are often full during the summer
explanation: The argument depends on the claim that a lack of parking keeps visitors away. If the existing 200 spaces are seldom full, parking is not what limits visitor numbers, and a new car park would bring few extra customers. (D) is the trap: cost bears on whether the project is worth paying for, but not on whether it would bring more business, which is what the council argues.

text: Fossil teeth of a prehistoric horse species from 8 million years ago have much taller crowns than teeth of the same species from 10 million years ago. Tall crowns allow teeth to withstand heavy wear, and grasses are far more gritty and wearing than the leaves of shrubs. Paleontologists conclude that grasslands spread through the region between 10 million and 8 million years ago.

stem: The paleontologists' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The horses of the region ate grass and no other kind of plant at all from 8 million years ago onward, in every season.
Tall-crowned teeth appeared in every grazing species in the region at the same time.
The extra wear on the horses' teeth was not caused mainly by dust settling on the leaves they already ate.
Grasslands today cover a larger share of the region than they did 8 million years ago.
Fossil teeth are more often preserved than other parts of horse skeletons.
explanation: The reasoning runs from taller crowns to heavier wear, and from heavier wear to a diet of grass. If the wear came mainly from dust on the same shrub leaves, the horses' teeth could have changed without any spread of grasslands, so the conclusion needs this possibility ruled out. (A) is too strong: grasslands could have spread even if the horses still ate some leaves.

text: Juniper Phones cut the price of its basic model by 20 percent, and in the following quarter sales of that model rose by 50 percent. The company's head of sales concludes that Juniper's customers are highly sensitive to price, and she recommends cutting the price of the company's premium model as well, expecting a similar rise in its sales. The basic model's features were not changed during the quarter.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the head of sales' conclusion that customers are highly sensitive to price?
options: The basic model still costs more than several rival phones with similar features.
In the same quarter, the leading rival basic phone was withdrawn from sale because of a battery defect.
Juniper's profit on each basic phone sold fell after the price was cut.
The premium model already sells more units than any rival company's premium model.
Sales of the basic model had already been rising slowly for a full year before its price was cut by Juniper.
explanation: If the main competing phone disappeared from shops that quarter, many buyers may have chosen Juniper because their first choice was unavailable, not because of the lower price. (E) is the trap: a slow existing rise cannot account for a sudden 50 percent jump. (C) concerns profit, which says nothing about how customers respond to price.

text: In the 1880s the port city of Valdora built a railway linking its harbor to the mining towns of the interior, expecting the amount of cargo passing through the harbor to grow. Over the following decade, the total tonnage of cargo shipped through the harbor did increase sharply. Yet the number of ships calling at the harbor each year fell during the same decade.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
options: The railway carried passengers as well as cargo between the harbor and the mining towns.
The mining towns produced considerably more ore in the 1890s than they had in the 1880s.
During that decade, shipping companies replaced many small sailing ships with far larger steamships.
Some of the goods from the mining towns were still carried down to the coast by road rather than by rail.
Several other harbors along the same coast also built railways to the interior in the 1880s.
explanation: More cargo carried by fewer ships is puzzling only if each ship carries about the same load. If small sailing ships were replaced by much larger steamships, each visit moved far more cargo, so total tonnage could rise while the number of ships fell. (B) explains why cargo increased, but not why fewer ships came.

text: A university's computer science department replaced the lectures in its introductory programming course with short online videos that students watch at home, and it now uses class time for supervised programming practice. In the first year of the new format, the share of students who passed the course's final exam rose from 68 percent to 81 percent. The head of the department argues that the new format improves students' learning.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department head's argument?
options: Students in the course said in surveys that they enjoyed the new format more than lectures.
Several other universities have replaced lectures with online videos in some of their courses.
The videos can be watched at any time of day and as often as a student wishes.
More students enrolled in the course in the first year of the new format than in the year before.
The exam was as hard as in past years, and the new students had similar entry grades to earlier ones.
explanation: A higher pass rate could come from an easier exam or stronger students rather than better learning. Ruling out both of those explanations leaves the new format as the most likely cause. (A) is the trap: enjoying a course is not the same as learning more from it.

text: In the country of Meridia, every household with a yearly income below 30,000 dollars qualifies for a heating subsidy, and every qualifying household is sent an application form. The subsidy, worth about 600 dollars a year, is paid only to households that return the form. Last winter, only half of the households that were sent the form returned it. Officials found that the households that returned it had, on average, the lowest incomes.

stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?
options: Most households in Meridia have yearly incomes below 30,000 dollars.
Households with incomes just below 30,000 dollars have no real need for the subsidy.
The application form is too complicated for many households to complete.
Some households that qualified for the subsidy last winter did not receive it.
Meridia spends more on heating subsidies than on any other kind of public assistance.
explanation: Every household sent the form qualified, the subsidy goes only to households that return it, and half did not return it, so some qualifying households went without the subsidy. (C) is a possible reason for the low return rate, but nothing in the passage establishes it, and (B) reads a motive into the pattern that the facts do not support.

text: Researchers at a coastal laboratory found that a strain of bacteria broke down plastic bottles twice as fast in seawater samples kept at 30°C as in samples kept at 15°C. Before testing, the samples were filtered to remove sand and other particles. The researchers propose releasing the bacteria into tropical seas, where the surface water is about 30°C, to clean up the plastic floating there.

stem: Which of the following, if true, casts the most serious doubt on the likely success of the researchers' proposal?
options: In the open sea, the bacteria are quickly eaten by tiny animals that the filtering had removed.
Some kinds of plastic sink below the sea's surface into water that is much colder than 30°C.
The bacteria break down plastic bottles more slowly than they break down plastic bags.
Plastic floating in tropical seas is often carried long distances by ocean currents.
The laboratory also tested the bacteria at 22°C and found a rate of breakdown between the other two.
explanation: The laboratory results come from filtered water, which lacked the small animals found in the open sea. If those animals quickly eat the bacteria, the bacteria will not survive long enough to break down much plastic, so the plan is unlikely to work. (B) is the trap: the proposal targets floating plastic, so plastic that sinks lies outside it.

text: Clinic director: Patients who visit our clinic's nutrition counselor lose more weight over the following six months than patients who do not. Last year, though, only 10 percent of our patients chose to visit the counselor. If we required every patient to see the counselor, the average weight loss among all our patients would rise substantially. Our counselor has years of experience, and patients who see her rate her very highly.

stem: The director's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
options: relies on figures from only a single year at a single clinic
overlooks that patients who choose to see the counselor may be more eager than others to lose weight
assumes that weight loss is the only sign of good health that matters to patients
fails to state how much each visit to the counselor would cost the clinic
confuses the number of patients who see the counselor with the number of separate visits that each patient makes
explanation: The patients who saw the counselor chose to go, so they may have been unusually motivated, and their motivation, not the counseling, may explain their greater weight loss. Patients forced to attend might gain little. (A) is a weaker objection: a single year of data can still be informative, and it does not address the real gap in the reasoning.

text: Last month, Brightline Logistics installed a new filter that blocks unwanted email before it reaches employees' inboxes. Since then, employees have reported receiving 70 percent fewer unwanted messages. The company's IT manager concludes that the filter is saving employees a large amount of working time, since they no longer have to read and delete so many unwanted messages each day.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the IT manager's conclusion?
options: The new filter cost the company less than the filter it replaced.
A few unwanted messages still reach most employees' inboxes every day.
Employees at Brightline receive considerably more email each day than employees at most similar firms do.
Employees now spend a long time each day searching the filter's folder for real messages it blocked by mistake.
Several other logistics companies in the region use the same filter.
explanation: The manager counts only the time saved by not deleting junk mail. If employees now spend a long time digging genuine messages out of the filter's folder, that new task may use up the time saved, or more. (B) is the trap: a few remaining unwanted messages are consistent with a 70 percent drop and a real saving of time.

text: A city health department found that neighborhoods in which fresh fruit stands opened had lower rates of childhood obesity five years later than similar neighborhoods without fruit stands. The department now plans to pay for more fruit stands in other neighborhoods, arguing that the stands improve children's diets and so help to prevent obesity. The stands sell fruit at about the same prices as local supermarkets do.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's argument?
options: School surveys show children near the new stands began eating more fruit and fewer sweets after the stands opened.
Most of the fruit stands were placed in neighborhoods that also gained new public parks and playgrounds during the same period.
The fruit stands are usually open only from early spring until late autumn.
Childhood obesity rates have fallen across the country during the past five years.
A few of the fruit stands closed within their first year because of low sales.
explanation: The argument claims that the stands work by improving children's diets. Evidence that children near the stands actually changed what they ate supports that link directly. (B) and (D) weaken the argument by offering other explanations for the lower obesity rates: new parks or a nationwide trend.

text: Letters written by the composer Anton Vasek mention a symphony that he finished in 1832, but no copy of its score has ever been found. A music historian claims that an unsigned score recently discovered in an archive in Prague is that lost symphony, because it is written on paper made in 1832 by the mill that supplied the paper for all of Vasek's other known scores.

stem: The historian's claim depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Vasek wrote more symphonies than any other composer of his time and region.
The unsigned score is the only unsigned score held in the Prague archive.
Vasek never wrote music on paper made by any mill other than this one.
The symphony mentioned in Vasek's letters was performed during his lifetime.
Few other composers of that time wrote their music on paper from the same mill.
explanation: The paper links the score to Vasek only if the mill's paper was not widely used by others; if many composers bought from the same mill, the score could be anyone's. (C) is too strong: the historian does not need Vasek to have used this mill exclusively, only for the paper to point to him rather than to many other composers.

text: Over the past three years, the number of customers using self-checkout machines at Petrov Supermarkets has doubled, and the chain has cut the number of cashiers it employs by more than a third. Yet over the same three years, the chain's total spending on store staff has risen, even though the number of its stores and their opening hours have not changed.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the rise in the chain's spending on store staff?
options: Customers who use the self-checkout machines tend to buy fewer items per visit than customers at staffed tills do.
Theft at the machines led the chain to hire supervisors to watch them, at higher wages than cashiers earn.
Buying and maintaining the self-checkout machines has cost the chain a great deal of money.
Wages for cashiers in the region rose slightly over the three years.
Several rival supermarket chains have also installed self-checkout machines in their stores.
explanation: Spending on staff can rise while cashier numbers fall if the chain is paying for new staff in other roles. Better-paid supervisors hired to prevent theft at the machines would do exactly that. (C) is the trap: the cost of the machines is equipment spending, not spending on staff, and (D) describes a slight rise that could not offset cutting more than a third of the cashiers.

text: ⟦Some astronomers have proposed that the unusual dimming of the star KX-14 is caused by a vast swarm of comets passing in front of it.⟧ If comets were responsible, however, the dimming would repeat in a regular pattern that followed the comets' orbits, and twenty years of observations show no such pattern. ⟦A more likely cause is dust from a recent collision between two planets⟧, since such dust spreads unevenly and would block the star's light at irregular intervals.

stem: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the conclusion that the argument defends; the second is a hypothesis that the argument rejects.
The first is evidence that the argument uses against a hypothesis; the second is that hypothesis.
The first is an explanation that the argument rejects; the second is the explanation it favors.
The first is an explanation that the argument rejects; the second is evidence offered against that explanation.
The first and the second are rival explanations, and the argument does not favor either of them.
explanation: The argument states the comet hypothesis and then rejects it because the expected regular pattern is missing. It then offers planetary dust as the more likely cause, which is its own conclusion. (D) is the trap: the second portion is not evidence against the comets but the rival explanation the argument prefers; the evidence against comets is the missing pattern.

text: Five years ago, Gallen City began requiring every new office building to include secure bicycle parking and showers for employees. Since then, the share of downtown workers who cycle to work has risen from 4 percent to 9 percent. The city's planning office credits the building rule with most of this increase and recommends extending it to new apartment buildings as well.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the planning office's conclusion?
options: The bicycle parking in many of the new office buildings is full by nine o'clock in the morning.
Some downtown workers who cycle to work drive instead on days when the weather is bad.
Building showers adds very little to the total cost of constructing a new office building.
Cycling to work is more common among younger workers in Gallen City than among older ones.
Over the same years, the city built a network of protected bike lanes from the suburbs to downtown.
explanation: A new network of safe bike lanes, built during the same five years, is a strong rival explanation for the rise in cycling, so the office cannot simply credit the building rule. (A) is the trap: full bicycle racks show that the parking is used, which if anything supports the office.

text: Nakamura Consulting offers a leadership course to employees who wish to move into management. Every employee who was promoted at the firm last year had completed the course. Half of the employees who completed the course, however, were not promoted. The firm admits to the course only employees who have worked there for at least three years. Promotions at the firm are decided once a year by a committee of partners.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Completing the leadership course makes an employee more likely to be promoted.
Half of the employees promoted last year had worked at the firm for more than three years.
Every employee promoted last year had worked at the firm for at least three years.
Some employees who had worked at the firm for less than three years were promoted last year.
Most of the firm's employees have completed the leadership course.
explanation: Everyone promoted had completed the course, and only employees with at least three years at the firm can take it, so everyone promoted had at least three years there. (A) is the trap: the passage gives no comparison with employees who skipped the course, so it does not show that the course raises anyone's chances. (D) contradicts the chain of statements.

text: For decades, browsing elk in Halden National Park ate nearly every young aspen along the park's streams. In the twelve years since wolves were reintroduced, aspen saplings there have rebounded sharply. Ecologists attribute the recovery less to the wolves' killing of elk than to a change in elk behavior: wary of ambush, the elk now avoid lingering on stream banks where approaching predators are hard to see.

stem: Which of the following would it be most useful to determine in evaluating the ecologists' explanation?
options: Whether aspens also rebounded at stream sites where elk can see predators approaching from far away
Whether elk in the park also browse on willow shrubs that grow beside the same streams
Whether wolves were reintroduced to other national parks during the same decade
Whether aspens grow more quickly along streams than on the dry hillsides of the park
Whether the reintroduced wolves were captured in a single region or in several different regions
explanation: The ecologists' explanation predicts that aspens should recover mainly where ambush is a danger, that is, where predators are hard to see. If aspens rebounded just as strongly at open sites with clear views, the fear-driven change in browsing would not explain the pattern, and a simple fall in elk numbers would look more likely. (B) is the trap: it concerns the elk's diet, but whether they also eat willows tells us nothing about why the aspens recovered.

text: In a large five-year trial, patients were randomly assigned either a new cholesterol drug or the standard one. The new drug lowered blood cholesterol considerably more than the standard drug did, and high cholesterol is a well-established cause of heart attacks. Nevertheless, patients taking the new drug suffered heart attacks at the same rate as those taking the standard drug, and both groups took their medication equally faithfully.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?
options: The new drug costs considerably more than the standard drug and is not yet widely available.
In large population studies, people with lower cholesterol have fewer heart attacks than other people.
Heart attacks were rarer in both groups of the trial than in the general population of the same age.
Apart from its effect on cholesterol, the standard drug attenuates inflammation of the arteries, which itself cuts the risk of heart attacks.
Doctors had expected the new drug to be about as effective as the standard drug at preventing heart attacks.
explanation: If the standard drug also protects the heart by a second route, reducing arterial inflammation, its patients gain a benefit that offsets the new drug's greater effect on cholesterol, so equal heart-attack rates make sense. "Attenuates" means weakens or reduces. (B) only restates why the result is surprising, and (C) compares both groups with outsiders without explaining why the two groups ended up equal.

text: Officials in Corvania plan to replace the toll booths on the country's highways with an electronic system that photographs each vehicle's license plate and mails a bill to its registered owner. Critics warn that many drivers will simply ignore the bills. The officials dismiss this worry: any unpaid tolls, they say, will be added to the fee that a vehicle's owner must pay to renew the vehicle's Corvanian registration each year.

stem: The officials' response to the critics depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Staffing the toll booths costs more than any other part of operating the highways.
Most of the vehicles that use Corvania's highways are registered in Corvania.
Most drivers would rather receive a bill by mail than stop at a toll booth.
The cameras can photograph license plates clearly in every kind of weather.
Drivers who are billed by mail will pay more promptly than they paid at the booths.
explanation: The officials' remedy works only for vehicles that renew a Corvanian registration. If most highway traffic consisted of vehicles registered abroad, unpaid tolls could not be collected this way, and the critics' worry would stand. (D) is the trap: clear photographs matter for issuing bills at all, but the question concerns the officials' answer to drivers who ignore bills they have received.
